paragraphs: Graph neural networks usually spread information through repeated exchanges between neighboring nodes. Information from distant parts of a graph must pass through many such exchanges, which can compress useful signals and make distant relationships difficult to capture. Global attention can address these problems, but its quadratic computational cost becomes expensive as graphs grow.

This paper introduces Graph ViT/MLP-Mixer, adapting architectures developed for computer vision to graph representation learning. The proposed models aim to capture distant relationships while keeping computational complexity linear in the number of nodes and edges. The authors also establish a graph-distinguishing capability expressed through the 3-WL graph-isomorphism criterion, giving a theoretical account of their representational power.

Experiments on four simulated datasets and seven real-world benchmarks show highly competitive results. Tests specifically targeting distant relationships and information compression support the intended benefits, while comparisons report better speed and memory efficiency than related graph transformers and expressive graph networks. Together, these findings support an alternative route to broad graph interactions without the quadratic cost associated with global attention.
icml-2023-a-generalization-of-vit-mlp-mi.tldr: Graph ViT/MLP-Mixer adapts vision architectures to capture distant graph relationships with linear computational complexity and strong graph-distinguishing ability.

paragraphs: An exploration bonus rewards an agent for encountering something unfamiliar. But unfamiliarity can be measured against its entire training history or only its current episode. When environments change between episodes, these two definitions can encourage different behavior. This paper investigates when each is useful through controlled, interpretable tasks and more challenging settings using pixel observations.

The experiments find that episodic bonuses are most effective when episodes share little structure, whereas global bonuses work well when more structure carries across episodes. The authors develop a conceptual explanation using variation in the value function across contexts. This connects the meaning of shared structure to how much the expected usefulness of states changes between environments.

Combining the bonuses can make performance more robust across different amounts of shared structure. The paper explores ways to define and combine them using function approximation, producing an algorithm that establishes a new state of the art on 16 previously used MiniHack tasks. It also performs robustly on Habitat and Montezuma’s Revenge, supporting the practical value of the combined approach.
icml-2023-a-study-of-global-and-episodic.tldr: Experiments explain when global or episodic exploration bonuses work best and show that combining them can improve robustness across changing environments.

paragraphs: Boosting combines classifiers that are individually only weakly accurate into a much more accurate predictor. AdaBoost is a classic way to do this and can achieve arbitrarily high accuracy when supplied with enough training data. The question examined here concerns how efficiently it uses those examples: does it need the smallest possible number to reach a desired accuracy?

A previously established weak-to-strong learning algorithm achieves provably optimal sample complexity, but its construction is comparatively complicated. That leaves a natural theoretical question about whether the familiar AdaBoost procedure already achieves the same efficiency. This paper resolves that question negatively by showing a gap between AdaBoost’s sample requirements and the optimal requirements.

The gap is at least a logarithmic factor in the desired accuracy, and the result also covers other classic variations of AdaBoost. This is a statement about sample efficiency, rather than a rejection of boosting’s ability to produce accurate classifiers. Its significance is that successful conversion from weak learning to strong learning does not by itself establish optimal use of training data.
icml-2023-adaboost-is-not-an-optimal-wea.tldr: AdaBoost and classic variants require at least a logarithmic factor more training samples than an optimal weak-to-strong learner.

paragraphs: A treatment policy governs both which treatments occur and when they occur. Future treatments may depend on earlier outcomes, so changing a policy involves more than choosing a fixed treatment sequence. This paper addresses causal questions about those policy changes, including cases where the original policy must first be estimated from observed treatment and outcome histories.

The authors jointly model treatments and outcomes in continuous time by combining Gaussian processes with point processes. Joint modeling allows the treatment process and the evolving outcome to be considered together. The model can estimate a treatment policy from observational sequences and predict outcome progression after an intervention changes that policy.

The approach supports both interventional and counterfactual queries about policy changes, extending the focus beyond the effect of an individual treatment. Evaluations using real-world and semi-synthetic blood glucose data show more accurate answers to causal queries than the alternatives considered. The central contribution is a framework that represents the policy generating treatments as part of the causal prediction problem.
icml-2023-causal-modeling-of-policy-inte.tldr: A continuous-time joint model of treatments and outcomes estimates treatment policies and predicts causal effects of changing them.

paragraphs: This paper studies nonlinear, nonconvex optimization with equality constraints, where solutions must improve an objective while satisfying prescribed equations. The proposed method uses Newton-style updates but avoids solving each associated linear system exactly. Instead, it uses randomized iterative sketching, which can reduce arithmetic and storage costs when suitable sketching matrices are chosen.

Approximate updates require care because an inaccurate direction may fail to improve the optimization criterion. The method adaptively adjusts both the randomized solver’s accuracy and the penalty parameters in an exact augmented Lagrangian. This coordination ensures a descent direction for that merit function, while a line search selects an appropriate step length.

The authors establish global almost sure convergence and local linear convergence, with full steps becoming admissible locally. Tightening the adaptive solver-accuracy condition progressively can strengthen the local rate to superlinear convergence. These convergence results should not be read as a promise of finding a global optimum in a nonconvex problem. Experiments report superior performance on benchmark nonlinear problems, constrained logistic regression, and a PDE-constrained problem.
icml-2023-constrained-optimization-via-e.tldr: An adaptive Newton method combines randomized approximate solves with an exact augmented Lagrangian to reduce costs while retaining convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning learns representations by deciding which examples should be treated as related. Existing approaches often construct different augmented views and use one-to-one positive pairs. This paper replaces that setup with neighborhood-based groups, while also addressing the difficulty of passing information between connected nodes that belong to different classes.

The central component is a parameterized neighbor sampler that maintains and updates neighbor sets. Those same sets guide both positive sampling for contrastive learning and message passing in the graph network. This connects two decisions that otherwise can be handled separately: which nodes provide related learning examples and which neighbors should contribute information to a node’s representation.

The authors call the resulting self-supervised approach group discrimination. They prove a mutual-information lower bound for unsupervised semantic learning and show that a lower bound can also be maintained with downstream tasks. Their experiments report substantial improvements over existing graph contrastive methods and efficient downstream fine-tuning. The stated explanation is that learned group selection addresses the homophily problem while improving the contrastive sampling strategy.
icml-2023-contrastive-learning-meets-hom.tldr: Learned neighbor groups jointly improve contrastive sampling and graph message passing, with mutual-information guarantees and reported empirical gains.

paragraphs: Counterfactual analysis asks how an outcome would have changed under a different action in a situation that already occurred. This becomes especially difficult when the system evolves over time and its underlying states are hidden. The paper develops an optimization framework that handles these two challenges together, rather than assuming the relevant state is directly observed.

The framework follows an abduction, action, and prediction structure: reason from observations about the underlying situation, change an action, and predict the resulting outcome. A central difficulty is that the causal mechanism is not fully known. There may be infinitely many possible mechanisms, so choosing a single mechanism would leave important uncertainty unresolved.

The authors optimize over the space of mechanisms to obtain lower and upper bounds on the counterfactual quantity of interest. The resulting interval expresses a range of counterfactual answers under that uncertainty. The framework brings together causal reasoning, state-space models, simulation, and optimization, and is applied in a breast cancer case study. The authors describe it as the first such bounding approach for dynamic latent-state models, to their knowledge.
icml-2023-counterfactual-analysis-in-dyn.tldr: An optimization framework bounds counterfactual outcomes in evolving systems with hidden states and uncertain causal mechanisms.

paragraphs: Polar codes support reliable communication, but decoding short blocks still leaves room for improvements in reliability and efficiency. This paper introduces CRISP, a sequential neural decoder trained using a deliberately designed curriculum. Its training strategy is guided by information-theoretic insights, making the organization of learning a central part of the proposed decoder.

CRISP outperforms successive-cancellation decoding and reaches near-optimal reliability on the Polar(32,16) and Polar(64,22) codes studied. Comparisons against other curricula show that the proposed curriculum is critical to the accuracy improvements. The findings therefore connect decoding quality to the training curriculum, rather than attributing the gains solely to adopting a neural model.

The approach also extends to Polarization-Adjusted-Convolutional, or PAC, codes, where existing successive-cancellation decoders are substantially less reliable. The authors report near-optimal performance on PAC(32,16) and describe CRISP as the first data-driven PAC decoder, to their knowledge. These results establish the method’s promise for the specified short codes while preserving the distinction between near-optimal reliability and exact optimality.
icml-2023-crisp-curriculum-based-sequent.tldr: CRISP uses an information-theoretically guided training curriculum to achieve near-optimal neural decoding reliability on selected short polar and PAC codes.

paragraphs: Learning actions from recorded interactions presents a tradeoff. Supervised imitation methods are robust but rely on optimal demonstrations, while offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning can use imperfect behavior but faces optimization difficulties. Distance Weighted Supervised Learning, or DWSL, seeks to combine supervised training with the ability to improve on the behavior present in offline data.

DWSL learns the full distribution of how many time steps separate states in the recorded data. It uses that distribution to approximate shortest-path distances, then weights actions according to how much they reduce the estimated distance to a goal. Both learning the distance information and extracting a policy use supervised learning, without bootstrapping.

The theoretical result establishes convergence to an optimal policy constrained to the data distribution. That qualification matters: optimality is tied to the available offline data. Empirically, DWSL at least matches behavior cloning across every tested dataset while also showing policy improvement. In image-based domains, it exceeds the performance of the prior goal-conditioned imitation and reinforcement learning methods considered.
icml-2023-distance-weighted-supervised-l.tldr: DWSL learns goal-reaching policies from offline data by supervising distance distributions and favoring actions that reduce estimated distance.

paragraphs: A time-series model transferred to a new domain may encounter changes in both signal structure and labels. Patterns can shift in their timing and frequency content, while the relative prevalence of labels can change or new labels can appear. RAINCOAT addresses these difficulties when the target domain has no labels available for adaptation.

The method considers temporal and frequency features together, aligns them between source and target domains, and corrects misalignments to help detect labels private to the target. It also identifies label shifts to improve transferability. This supports both closed-set adaptation, where the label sets match, and universal adaptation, where the method must accommodate differences between those sets.

Experiments across five datasets and comparisons with 13 existing adaptation methods show transfer-learning improvements of up to 16.33%. This figure is a reported maximum, rather than an improvement promised for every transfer. The results support the value of addressing signal changes and label changes together, and demonstrate that RAINCOAT can handle both adaptation settings within the proposed approach.
icml-2023-domain-adaptation-for-time-ser.tldr: RAINCOAT adapts time-series models to unlabeled domains by jointly addressing temporal and frequency feature shifts and changes in labels.

paragraphs: Some biologically motivated learning methods update networks using differences between activities in two inferred states. Solving the inference problem twice makes these approaches costly on digital hardware. Even in analog settings, where equilibrium propagation may offer speed and energy advantages, the need to infer and store two states remains a challenge.

Dual propagation redesigns the neuron so that it contains two intrinsic states within a single energy-based model. Their difference represents error, while their mean represents activity. This arrangement brings the two kinds of information into one inference phase. The paper also shows that inference can be computed through layerwise closed-form solutions, addressing another source of computational expense.

Experiments on common computer vision datasets, including ImageNet32x32, find performance equivalent to backpropagation in both accuracy and runtime. These findings support the practical benefit of changing the neuron representation and inference procedure together. The contribution is an experimentally competitive activity-difference learning approach that avoids the two separate inference phases responsible for much of the earlier computational burden.
icml-2023-dual-propagation-accelerating-.tldr: Dual propagation encodes activity and error in two-state neurons, enabling one inference phase and experimentally matching backpropagation’s accuracy and runtime.

paragraphs: For data generated by a smooth process, useful information includes the shape and continuity of the signal. A recognizable pattern may also matter regardless of where it appears. This paper develops functional neural networks to incorporate both ideas: preserving smoothness and recognizing signals independently of their position.

The authors use tools from functional data analysis to extend multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks to functional data. This treats the observations through their underlying functional structure. They propose multiple architectures within this class, with shift invariance and preservation of smoothness as defining properties. The approach makes those desired behaviors part of the model design.

The reported evaluations show higher accuracy than a benchmark model from functional data analysis, and the networks are successfully applied to EEG classification. These results support combining neural-network architectures with the structure emphasized by functional analysis. The stated comparison establishes an improvement over the evaluated FDA benchmark, while the EEG application demonstrates that the models can be used on recorded brain-signal data.
icml-2023-functional-neural-networks-shi.tldr: Functional neural networks preserve signal smoothness and recognize patterns across shifts, with improved accuracy over an FDA benchmark and successful EEG classification.

paragraphs: Physical equations can constrain which predictions are plausible. This paper builds those constraints directly into Gaussian process priors: for any system of linear partial differential equations with constant coefficients, every realization of the proposed prior is an exact solution. The resulting family, EPGP, therefore represents uncertainty within the space of solutions to the specified equations.

The construction uses the Ehrenpreis-Palamodov fundamental principle, described as functioning like a nonlinear Fourier transform, to build kernels in the spirit of spectral Gaussian process methods. These priors can infer probable solutions from noisy measurements or pointwise initial and boundary conditions. The authors also provide a sparse version, S-EPGP, that learns relevant spectral frequencies and works better with large datasets.

Demonstrations cover the heat equation, wave equation, and Maxwell’s equations. The authors report improvements over the state of the art in computation time and precision, reaching several orders of magnitude in some experiments. The general construction applies to linear systems with constant coefficients; its exact-solution guarantee is specifically tied to that stated equation class.
icml-2023-gaussian-process-priors-for-sy.tldr: EPGP constructs Gaussian process priors whose realizations exactly satisfy specified linear PDE systems with constant coefficients.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a chaotic system from time series means learning its geometry and persistent temporal properties, including structures such as attractors. Training recurrent networks for this purpose is difficult because chaotic trajectories diverge exponentially, producing exploding gradients. The paper also seeks compact reconstructions, since lower-dimensional, mathematically tractable models are desirable for scientific interpretation.

The authors introduce a simple modification of teacher forcing and prove that it keeps training gradients bounded at all times. They pair this training change with an architectural rearrangement of piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks. Together, these modifications allow faithful reconstruction in spaces whose dimensionality is no greater than that of the observed system.

Across several dynamical systems, the proposed approach reconstructs dynamics better than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered while using substantially fewer dimensions. The reported differences are especially compelling on real-world data, where most competing methods struggle. The contribution connects stable training with compact modeling: controlling gradients helps make a tractable recurrent architecture useful for reconstructing chaotic behavior without relying on a much larger state representation.
icml-2023-generalized-teacher-forcing-fo.tldr: Modified teacher forcing guarantees bounded training gradients and, with a revised recurrent architecture, enables compact reconstructions of chaotic dynamics.

paragraphs: Visual recognition requires both nearby details and relationships across an image. Global Context Vision Transformer, or GC ViT, combines local self-attention with global-context attention to model these two scales efficiently. The architecture avoids expensive operations such as attention-mask computation and shifted local windows, aiming to make better use of parameters and computation.

The model also incorporates modified fused inverted residual blocks to introduce useful structural biases into the vision transformer. Its design therefore addresses both information exchange across spatial distances and the architectural assumptions that guide visual learning. The authors evaluate the resulting architecture on classification and use pretrained backbones for detection and segmentation tasks.

On ImageNet-1K at 224 resolution without pretraining, variants with 51 million, 90 million, and 201 million parameters achieve 84.3%, 85.0%, and 85.7% top-1 accuracy, respectively. The paper reports state-of-the-art results across the evaluated task families and consistent downstream improvements on MS COCO and ADE20K. These findings support the proposed combination of local interactions, global context, and architectural bias as an effective visual backbone.
icml-2023-global-context-vision-transfor.tldr: GC ViT combines local and global-context attention with structural visual biases, reporting strong efficiency and state-of-the-art vision results.

paragraphs: Fourier neural operators work in the frequency domain to help solve partial differential equations. The paper asks how these models can incorporate symmetries associated with changes of coordinates. If an input is rotated, translated, or reflected, an equivariant model transforms its output correspondingly, making those relationships part of its architecture.

The authors extend group convolutions into the frequency domain and use the Fourier transform’s equivariance properties to construct suitable layers. This produces G-FNO, a Fourier neural operator designed to respect rotations, translations, and reflections. The work addresses a gap between well-studied symmetry methods in physical space and less-explored symmetry handling in frequency-based models.

The reported results show that G-FNO generalizes well across input resolutions and performs well in settings with different levels of symmetry. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating symmetry directly into Fourier layers. They also indicate that the architecture can remain effective across the varied symmetry settings evaluated, connecting a mathematical design principle with practical behavior on PDE problems.
icml-2023-group-equivariant-fourier-neur.tldr: G-FNO builds rotation, translation, and reflection equivariance into Fourier layers and reports good performance across resolutions and varying symmetry levels.

paragraphs: Different measures of model quality need not respond to increasing input dimension in the same way. This paper studies that issue for uncertainty estimation with Gaussian processes, focusing on marginal likelihood and cross-validation. It challenges the expectation that both measures should behave similarly and deteriorate as more input dimensions are introduced.

Under the theoretical setting studied, tuning hyperparameters to maximize marginal likelihood makes performance measured by that same criterion improve monotonically with dimension. Cross-validation measures instead show behavior characteristic of double descent. The distinction matters because improvement in a model-selection criterion does not establish that a separate predictive evaluation measure follows the same trend.

Cold posteriors appear to intensify these effects, preserving the paper’s qualified claim about their role. Experiments also find the predicted behavior on real data beyond the assumptions used in the analysis, and the authors examine consequences involving synthetic covariates. Together, the results show why conclusions about dimensionality depend on which uncertainty-related performance measure is being examined and how hyperparameters are selected.
icml-2023-monotonicity-and-double-descen.tldr: For the analyzed Gaussian processes, optimized marginal likelihood improves with dimension while cross-validation exhibits double-descent behavior.

paragraphs: Related decision tasks can contain useful information about one another. This paper studies how to exploit those relationships when learning policies from logged bandit feedback, where the available records describe actions already taken and their observed outcomes. Its motivating settings include users with similar preferences and items with similar affinities.

The proposed algorithm, HierOPO, organizes tasks in a hierarchy whose shared relationships are captured through an unknown latent parameter. It estimates task parameters using this structure and then chooses actions pessimistically with respect to those estimates. This combines information sharing across tasks with caution about what the estimated parameters support.

The authors develop Bayesian error bounds that improve as the prior becomes more informative and explicitly capture statistical gains from the hierarchy. They describe these as the first off-policy bounds with those properties. Experiments also demonstrate benefits over solving each task independently. The theoretical and empirical contributions align around the same idea: related tasks can improve learning efficiency when their shared structure is represented in the learning procedure.
icml-2023-multi-task-off-policy-learning.tldr: HierOPO shares information through a task hierarchy and acts pessimistically, with Bayesian bounds and experiments supporting improved off-policy learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in episodic linear Markov decision processes. The key structural assumption is that transition probabilities are linear functions of a given feature mapping, while the dynamics may vary across steps within an episode. The objective is to learn efficiently while controlling regret, the accumulated cost of acting below optimal performance.

The proposed computationally efficient algorithm uses weighted linear regression with weights determined by a new variance estimator. That estimator directly targets the variance of the optimal value function and decreases monotonically as episodes accumulate. A rare-switching policy limits updates to the value-function estimator, helping control the complexity of the class of estimates involved in learning.

The resulting regret bound is nearly minimax optimal: up to logarithmic factors, it scales as d times the square root of H cubed times K, where d is feature dimension, H is horizon, and K is episode count. The contribution combines near-optimal statistical performance with computational efficiency for this specified model class, rather than asserting an optimal solution for unrestricted reinforcement learning.
icml-2023-nearly-minimax-optimal-reinfor.tldr: A computationally efficient weighted-regression algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret for episodic linear Markov decision processes.

paragraphs: Multi-resolution hash encoding reduces the computational cost of neural rendering, but it depends on accurate camera positions and orientations. Simply applying gradient-based camera refinement alongside this representation can severely degrade performance. This paper investigates that failure and proposes a method that jointly calibrates camera poses and learns scene geometry using the efficient hash representation.

The authors identify oscillating gradient flows in hash encoding as an obstacle to camera registration. Their method uses smooth interpolation weighting to stabilize these oscillations when rays are sampled across hash grids. This targets the optimization signal used to refine the cameras, addressing the interaction between pose estimation and the scene representation.

A curriculum training procedure also helps the model learn the encoding at different levels, further improving pose refinement. Experiments on novel-view synthesis datasets report state-of-the-art performance and rapid convergence. The findings show that retaining an efficient rendering representation requires adapting the joint optimization procedure to its gradient behavior, with interpolation smoothing and curriculum training contributing to the proposed solution.
icml-2023-robust-camera-pose-refinement-.tldr: Smooth interpolation and curriculum training stabilize joint camera-pose refinement and scene learning with multi-resolution hash encoding.

paragraphs: Nyström approximation represents a kernel using selected landmark points and an associated lower-dimensional subspace. This paper analyzes the approximation of a positive definite kernel tied to a probability measure. Its focus is on understanding approximation error and improving how the representing subspace is selected, including when landmark sampling differs from the conventional independent setup.

The first result improves the error bound for conventional Nyström approximation using independently sampled landmarks and singular-value decomposition in the continuous setting. The proof draws on statistical learning theory. The authors then introduce a refined subspace-selection method with theoretical guarantees that also apply to landmark points that are not independently and identically distributed.

Finally, the paper connects these approximation results to convex kernel quadrature, where kernel methods support numerical integration. It supplies new theoretical guarantees for that application alongside numerical observations. The contribution links two questions: how accurately sampled landmarks represent a kernel, and how that representation can support integration. Its guarantees extend the analysis beyond one standard sampling arrangement without claiming unrestricted accuracy for every landmark choice.
icml-2023-sampling-based-nystrom-approxi.tldr: The paper strengthens Nyström error guarantees, refines subspace selection for non-i.i.d. landmarks, and applies the results to kernel quadrature.

paragraphs: Distinct counting estimates how many unique elements appear in data that may contain repeated values. Compact summaries, called sketches, make this operation efficient, and merging sketches lets a system summarize unions of datasets. This paper addresses the difficulty of retaining that useful merging capability while providing differential privacy.

The authors propose cardinality sketches that combine mergeability, differential privacy, and low empirical error. A central ingredient is a randomized algorithm for performing logical operations on noisy bits. That mechanism supports operations needed for merging while accommodating the noise involved in privacy protection. The paper also provides a tight privacy analysis and a provably optimal estimation procedure.

Simulations and experiments on real-world data show that the proposed sketches substantially outperform existing theoretical solutions. The practical significance is the simultaneous availability of compact counting, private summaries, and merging, which are valuable together in data warehouses. The empirical error findings complement the formal privacy and estimation results, showing how the proposed construction behaves in the evaluated counting tasks.
icml-2023-sketch-flip-merge-mergeable-sk.tldr: Sketch-Flip-Merge provides mergeable, differentially private distinct-counting sketches with formal estimation guarantees and low observed errors.

paragraphs: Stacking learns how to combine predictions from several base models by treating those predictions as inputs to another learner. Although widely used, the theoretical behavior of choosing a stacking strategy is less well understood. This paper studies whether cross-validation can reliably select among a family of such strategies.

The authors prove that selecting the best cross-validated strategy from a finite or finite-dimensional family does not perform much worse than the oracle-best choice in that family. The oracle is the comparison point representing the best available candidate. This supports selection within the specified family; it does not claim that every possible ensemble or unrestricted collection is covered.

Guided by the analysis, the authors propose a family of stacking methods for probabilistic forecasting. Members differ in how freely ensemble weights vary across forecasted items, future timestamps, and quantiles. This makes the flexibility of the combination itself a selectable property. Experiments demonstrate performance gains, linking the theoretical selection guarantee to a concrete forecasting approach with different degrees of weight variation.
icml-2023-theoretical-guarantees-of-lear.tldr: Cross-validation receives an oracle-comparison guarantee for selecting stacking strategies, motivating flexible ensembles for probabilistic forecasting.

paragraphs: Active learning selects which examples should receive labels so that a model can learn effectively from a limited labeled set. This paper adds a second objective to predictive quality: reducing sensitivity to the neural network’s random initial parameters. That concern matters when different training initializations could otherwise yield inconsistent predictive behavior.

The authors introduce EV-GP, an expected-variance criterion based on Gaussian processes. They provide a theoretical guarantee connecting its selections to both good predictive performance and robustness to initialization in trained neural networks. The selection process does not require training the neural network, making it computationally efficient. Training-free here describes choosing data; the selected examples are still used to train the resulting network.

Empirically, EV-GP is strongly correlated with both generalization performance and initialization robustness. The method consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines on both objectives, particularly when the initial labeled set is small or selection batches are large. The contribution treats stable outcomes across initializations as an explicit data-selection objective alongside predictive accuracy.
icml-2023-training-free-neural-active-le.tldr: EV-GP selects labeling candidates without neural-network training, with theoretical and empirical support for predictive performance and initialization robustness.

paragraphs: Theoretical analyses often simplify neural networks by letting their width become infinite before considering infinite depth. But actual networks can have width and depth of comparable size, raising the question of whether that order of analysis is informative. This paper examines the issue for networks with skip connections under a specific scaling of their residual branches.

When branches are scaled by the inverse square root of depth, the authors show that the limiting covariance structure is the same regardless of how width and depth approach infinity. Covariance describes relationships among the network’s signals. The result explains why the conventional width-first analysis can still provide insight when depth grows on the same order as width.

The paper also establishes Gaussian distributions for pre-activations in this setting, with direct relevance to Bayesian deep learning. Extensive simulations closely match the theoretical predictions. The branch scaling is central to the stated result: the paper establishes agreement of these limits for the specified residual-network setup, rather than asserting that width and depth limits commute for every neural architecture.
icml-2023-width-and-depth-limits-commute.tldr: With residual branches scaled by inverse square-root depth, infinite-width and infinite-depth limits yield the same covariance structure regardless of their order.
